newsitem.title: USA: US Sen Lugar sees lower cost, large CRP.
newsitem.headline: US Sen Lugar sees lower cost, large CRP.

text.p: The U.S. Conservation Reserve will emerge as a lower cost, more environmentally targeted program when results of the latest sign-up are announced, Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar said Tuesday.
Lugar told reporters he believed Agriculture Department would accept more than 14 million acres from the 25.6 million that were offered but had no likely figure for enrollment.
"I'm led to believe we're going to see a rent figure per acre that is substantially less than the rent the federal government is now paying," said Lugar, Indiana Republican.
Lugar said there also were indications "that we're going to see a larger percentage of the acreage in what might be called environmentally impacted or challenged land."
"I'm also led to believe the geographic dispersion is going to be roughly the same," he said.

USDA pays about $50 an acre for the 32 million acres now in the Conservation Reserve Program. This fall, the CRP will undergo the biggest turnover of acreage in its history. Contracts on 21 million acres expire.
Announcement was expected later this week of USDA decision on how much land to accept overall and in each state.
Currently, the Plains and Midwest dominate CRP acreage.
"The number of acres, we think, is still up rather than down, given the waylaying of the (14 million-acre) cap on CRP acreage that appeared to be happening in House legislation," Lugar said.

Asked if lawmakers might again try to limit CRP acreage, Lugar said, "Much depends on how the sign-up works." The House cap was inspired by fears among Northeasterners that too little attention would be paid to water quality work.
Lugar said he would not object to a high acreage total for CRP entry, provided conservation goals were met.
"I would hope we would have a very large CRP program. That has always been my intent," he said.
